verdict.reason: Ikuhara's surreal anime masterpiece transforms Revolutionary Girl Utena into pure cinema. The film's visual complexity rewards the big screen treatment it rarely receives.

ratings.plot: During WWII, Soviet orphan Ivan Bondarev strikes up a friendship with three sympathetic Soviet officers while working as a scout behind the German lines.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing for Tarkovsky's debut feature, which establishes his visual language decades before his later masterpieces. The dream sequences and birch forest cinematography create images that burn into memory long after the credits roll.

ratings.plot: A truck driver stops at a small family-run noodle shop and decides to help its fledgling business. The story is intertwined with various vignettes about the relationship of love and food.

verdict.reason: See Itami's ramen western on the biggest screen you can find. The film's obsessive food cinematography and precise comic timing demand theatrical viewing.

ratings.plot: Autumn Moon (Sam Lee), a low-rent triad living in Hong Kong, struggles to find meaning in his hopelessly violent existence.

verdict.reason: One of the essential films of Hong Kong's handover period that deserves a big screen viewing. Chan shoots with handheld 16mm that captures the raw energy of street-level desperation better than any digital transfer.

movies.title: DAYS AND NIGHTS IN THE FOREST

verdict.reason: Essential Ray on the big screen — this ranks among his finest character studies. The Metrograph restoration reveals the subtle interplay between natural light and psychological insight that makes his camera work irreplaceable.

ratings.plot: Eight-year-old Ahmed has mistakenly taken his friend Mohammad's notebook. He wants to return it, or else his friend will be expelled from school. The boy determinedly sets out to find Mohammad's home in the neighbouring village.

verdict.reason: Kiarostami's breakthrough transforms a simple premise into profound cinema. The Iranian landscape and natural light create images that lose impact on small screens.

ratings.plot: A magazine tycoon commits a murder and pins it on an innocent man, who then tries to solve the murder himself.

verdict.reason: This is essential noir viewing with Ray Milland trapped in a corporate nightmare of his own making. Farrow builds the tension around a literal ticking clock that becomes both plot device and visual metaphor for corporate paranoia.

ratings.plot: To avoid the heat of a sweltering summer night a 9-year-old Manhattan boy decides to sleep on the fire escape and witnesses a murder, but no one will believe him.

verdict.reason: Essential noir that proves children can anchor suspense as effectively as adults. Tetzlaff shoots the tenement fire escapes and rooftops like a urban jungle where every shadow hides danger.

ratings.plot: An unethical lawyer who wants to help his older brother becomes a partner with a client in the numbers racket.

verdict.reason: Essential noir that holds up as one of the best films about American corruption. Polonsky's direction turns New York into a concrete jungle where every shadow hides moral decay.

ratings.plot: Pulp novelist Holly Martins travels to shadowy, postwar Vienna, only to find himself investigating the mysterious death of an old friend, Harry Lime.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing on the big screen where Reed's tilted camera angles and deep focus photography can work their full magic. The zither music and Vienna's bombed-out sewers create an atmosphere that streaming cannot match.

ratings.plot: Paddington, now happily settled with the Brown family and a popular member of the local community, picks up a series of odd jobs to buy the perfect present for his Aunt Lucy's 100th birthday, only for the gift to be stolen.

ratings.plot: A family of six settles into their new home on Vancouver Island as internal dynamics are slowly revealed through the eyes of the youngest child.

verdict.reason: See this intimate family portrait while it has theatrical momentum. Romvari shoots through a child's perspective with uncommon sensitivity to how kids actually process adult tensions.

movies.title: Marcel the Shell with Shoes On

ratings.plot: A cash-strapped documentary maker decides to make his newest documentary about a mollusk shell he finds living in his Airbnb with his friends.

verdict.reason: This deserves the biggest screen you can find for a film that transforms intimate stop-motion into genuine magic. Fleischer Camp's direction makes Marcel's tiny world feel vast and emotionally enormous.

ratings.plot: A powerful Broadway columnist coerces an unscrupulous press agent into breaking up his sister's romance with a jazz musician.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing for anyone who wants to see Hollywood noir at its most vicious and articulate. Mackendrick and cinematographer James Wong Howe turn Times Square into a neon-lit hell that makes every frame crackle with menace.

ratings.plot: A father fights fiercely against ruthless kidnappers to save his abducted daughter.

verdict.reason: See this revenge thriller on the biggest screen you can find. Tanigaki's stunt choreography background delivers car chases and fight sequences that demand theatrical sound and scale.

ratings.plot: Viridiana, a young nun about to take her final vows, pays a visit to her widowed uncle at the request of her Mother Superior.

verdict.reason: Buñuel's scandalous masterpiece that got him banned from Spain, worth seeing for the Last Supper parody sequence. The film's blasphemous imagery retains its power to shock and provoke.

movies.title: Double Feature: Blues in The Night & Black Angel

ratings.plot:
Double Feature!


BLUES IN THE NIGHT

The first noir film to delve into the jazz world, Blues in the Night details the rise and inevitable fall of a St. Louis band. They land their big break when they get booked at a New Jersey nightclub, but the band’s leader, played by Richard Whorf, falls under the spell of the club’s femme fatale owner. It doesn’t take long for the other members to sour, setting off a chain reaction of jealousy, betrayal, and, eventually, murder. The supporting cast is superb, made up of familiar noir faces like Jack Carson, Howard Da Silva and Lloyd Nolan, while the screenplay by Robert Rossen makes good on the lyrics of the tragic, Oscar®-nominated title song. Future director Elia Kazan has his biggest movie role as the band’s clarinetist.



BLACK ANGEL

Kirk Bennett is sentenced to die for the murder of gorgeous actress Mavis Marlowe (Constance Dowling), but his wife (June Vincent) won’t give up trying to prove his innocence. She desperately enlists the aid of Marty Blair (Dan Duryea), a pickled pianist on the skids who happens to be the victim’s husband! The amateur sleuths go undercover as a performing duo, tracing clues to a ritzy Sunset Strip nightclub run by shady operator Marko (Peter Lorre). Bringing extra heat is Broderick Crawford as a dogged LAPD police captain. As usual in Woolrich stories, things aren’t what they seem—leading to one of the writer’s most memorable and unexpected climaxes. Known for his smarmy, villainous turns in many films of the period, here Duryea had his first role as a leading man in one of the era’s best adaptations of a novel by Cornell Woolrich, the undisputed master of noir fiction. Featuring fantastic art direction by Martin Obzina and inventive camerawork by Paul Ivano.

verdict.reason: Two solid noirs for the price of one, with the rare chance to see future Kazan in front of the camera. The three-hour commitment pays off with Duryea's best leading man performance and some of the sharpest Cornell Woolrich plotting on film.

“The most sickly entertaining theatrical experience of the year.” – IndieWire Oh, the things we do for beauty. Look, we’re not saying we wouldn’t want to look like Margaret Qualley, but Demi Moore’s over-the-hill aerobic star goes to some pretty extreme measures. Her use of THE SUBSTANCE may transform her into a “younger, more beautiful, more perfect” version of herself (via a gloriously horrific rebirth), but the more she uses it, the worse the side effects become. It becomes increasingly apparent that beauty is only skin deep as both of her lives spiral into a truly ugly mess. THE SUBSTANCE is a wild, toe-curling ride from writer/director Coralie Fargeat that features some of the most nerve-shredding body horror sequences in recent years. And with it taking home the award for Best Screenplay at the 2024 Cannes Film Festival, there’s plenty of substance behind the camera as well. As fantastical as the beauty solution is, THE SUBSTANCE’s themes of aging, youth, and self-esteem are very much grounded in our obsession with physical beauty.

In this charming little parlor, you don't just get your hair and nails did – you get life lessons from some of the best and sassiest actresses to ever grace the screen. Without STEEL MAGNOLIAS, how would you know that there are so many different shades of pink (including Blush and Bashful), or that all gay men have track lighting? Without Ouiser Boudreaux (Shirley MacLaine, in all of her cantankerously awesome glory), how would you discover that it's possible to be in a bad mood for 40 years? And without Clairee Belcher (Olympia Dukakis), how would you learn that the only thing that separates us from animals is our ability to accessorize? Don't even get us started on Truvy Jones (Dolly Parton), whose folksy wisdom and bedazzled ensembles basically make life worth living. These ladies are guaranteed to inspire you just as sure as they'll make you bawl your eyes out and then crack you up, because we all know laughter through tears is the best emotion. So tease up your hair, grab your bestie, and join us for a cinematic celebration of friendship, perms, and Southern living. It'll be even better than a slice of armadillo cake.

Watched by audiences of over 3.5 million, SIX the Musical has become a global theatre phenomenon since its 2017 debut at Edinburgh Festival Fringe, where it has redefined the boundaries of musical theatre. verdict.reason: Worth it if you love the show enough to sing along in public, but the theatrical energy gets lost in translation to cinema. The original West End cast delivers the vocals with precision, but filmed musicals rarely capture what makes live theater electric.

ratings.plot: When 13 GOING ON 30 was released over 20 years ago(!), I was overjoyed at the fact that Hollywood had finally decided to make BIG for girls. This film features the greatest fantasies of a 13-year-old girl*: a makeover montage in a gigantic closet, a high-power job working at a fashion magazine, a massive slumber party, and, of course, a totally cute guy. But 13 GOING ON 30 isn't just a fun premise, it's a heartfelt and hilarious coming-of-age story. The cast is top-notch, with Garner perfectly embodying her inner teen, Judy Greer serving up some major sass (like she does), and Mark Ruffalo being as foxy and charming as he's ever been. This delightful cinematic concoction is better than a pack of Razzles, so join us and experience the thrill of being 30, flirty, and thriving. *Or any girl, regardless of her age.
